target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, work efficiency, accessibility for disabled people, and workplace safety.
objection: AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses, undermines critical thinking for students and adults, worsens outcomes for racial minorities by repeating and amplifying racism, and creates dangerous privacy risks; therefore AI is not good for society.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy risks make AI broadly unsafe and socially bad.
objection: AI privacy harms are not inherent: they come from how data is collected, stored, and accessed, so privacy-preserving governance, data minimization, and privacy controls can substantially reduce exposure.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily repeats and exacerbates racism.
objection: AI bias is often caused by biased training data and evaluation practices, and fairness testing, better data selection, and corrective modeling can reduce racist patterns in outputs.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking for students and adults.
objection: AI can be used as an assistive learning tool that prompts users to explain and verify reasoning, so with proper instructional design it can support independent judgment rather than weaken it.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily harms the economy.
objection: Economic harms from AI depend partly on workforce transition policies; reskilling and job-support programs can reduce disruption, while productivity gains can raise overall living standards.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy, bias, critical-thinking, and economic harms can be largely solved by design and governance.
objection: In practice, AI systems often infer sensitive traits from ordinary data, bias persists across deployment contexts and feedback loops despite mitigation, users frequently do not carefully verify outputs, and reskilling programs are too limited to offset rapid automation at scale; therefore these harms are not generally eliminated by mitigation.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy, bias, critical-thinking, and economic harms are unavoidable and make AI categorically bad.
objection: Those harms are strongly tied to particular deployment patterns—such as surveillance-heavy systems, high-stakes automation, using AI as a substitute for verification, and automation without transition planning—rather than to AI itself.

target: AG1’s claim that harmful AI deployment patterns can be avoided while still gaining benefits at scale.
objection: AI applications that improve health, living standards, and workplace safety at scale typically require large-scale data collection and consequential automated prediction or risk scoring, so the same deployment patterns that create privacy and discrimination risks are often necessary for the purported benefits; avoiding the harms while still getting the benefits at scale is not practically possible.

target: AG2’s claim that accessibility and workplace-safety AI still require the same high-risk data regime that drives the privacy objection.
objection: Major accessibility and workplace-safety applications can operate on user-side or on-site signals instead of broad surveillance databases, so the opponent’s privacy argument does not straightforwardly apply to all important welfare-improving uses of AI.

target: AG1’s claim that accessibility and workplace-safety AI can avoid the privacy/sensitive-data regime.
objection: Mainstream accessibility and workplace-safety AI systems often rely on extensive biometric or behavioral monitoring, which enables sensitive-trait inference and operates within the very regime of data collection and inference that creates privacy risk; therefore these use cases do not reliably avoid the high-risk data regime.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s economic effects are broadly negative because automation displaces workers.
objection: AI can raise productivity, lower costs, and create complementary demand for human labor in oversight, maintenance, integration, training, and customer support, so aggregate employment and incomes need not be net-harmed.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines students’ critical thinking because users will defer to outputs.
objection: AI tutoring can be designed to require step-by-step explanations and source-grounded, verifiable claims, which incentivizes students to check and reason about outputs rather than passively accept them.

target: AG1’s claim that verification-based AI tutoring can scale and strengthen critical thinking.
objection: High-quality verification-based tutoring would require costly per-interaction checking of reasoning and citations, which becomes prohibitive at scale; when verification is sparse or unreliable, students will game the system and defer to AI, so such tutoring cannot realistically be deployed widely enough to reliably improve critical thinking.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms to marginalized groups outweigh its benefits for them.
objection: AI assistive technologies expand accessibility for people with disabilities and enable fuller participation in education, work, and daily life, so inclusion benefits for marginalized groups are a major societal good.

target: AG1’s claim that accessibility AI reliably benefits disabled users overall.
objection: Accessibility AI often processes sensitive disability-related data and can expose users to privacy harms, and it can perform worse for users with speech, hearing, or motor impairments, producing unreliable outputs that create practical exclusion; therefore AI assistive tools can reverse inclusion gains for some disabled users.

target: AG2’s claim that AI cannot be good because of harms, using public health as an example of benefit.
objection: AI can forecast disease outbreaks and optimize medical resources, reducing illness and death rates and improving health and living standards at the societal level.

target: AG1’s claim that AI in public-health and emergency-response decisions reliably improves health outcomes.
objection: Those applications require sensitive health/location data, creating privacy exposure that can interfere with reporting and response, can misdirect resources in racially unequal ways, and can encourage over-reliance on AI in high-stakes judgments; therefore AI in these settings does not reliably reduce illness and death and can worsen health outcomes.

target: AG1’s claim that AI adoption need not harm the economy because smaller firms can access AI through pretrained models and cloud services.
objection: AI development and deployment usually require large-scale data and compute, which advantages big firms and creates barriers for smaller businesses, reducing competition, job creation, and business survival; therefore AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses.

target: AG2’s claim that access via pretrained models, open-source tools, or cloud APIs does not prevent smaller firms from competing.
objection: Many AI applications can be built with pretrained models, open-source tooling, and cloud/API providers without each firm owning major infrastructure, so AI adoption does not inherently require concentration among only large corporations.

target: AG1’s claim that APIs and multiple providers prevent concentration and keep AI economically beneficial.
objection: Even with API access, firms can become dependent on a few providers that control models, pricing, updates, and interfaces; that dependence creates switching costs and concentrates power, weakening bargaining power and job security and harming the economic well-being of many people and businesses.

target: AG2’s claim that provider dependence makes AI economically harmful overall.
objection: In real markets, firms can often use multiple providers or open-source/self-hosted alternatives, and AI productivity gains can lower costs, expand output, and create complementary labor demand, so AI’s net economic effects need not be negative.

target: AG1’s claim that competition and multiple providers will prevent concentration from persisting.
objection: AI markets are technically opaque, making dominance and anticompetitive conduct hard to detect and remedy quickly; once advantages emerge, reinforcing data feedback loops and winner-take-most concentration can persist and shrink opportunities for smaller firms and workers.

target: AG2’s claim that concentration is inevitable and will harm the economy.
objection: AI markets are often open enough that firms can choose among providers and compete on application-layer differentiation, while productivity and cost savings can raise living standards and create complementary work even when some firms gain data advantages.

target: AG1’s claim that concentration is not inevitable because markets remain competitive.
objection: Because AI markets are opaque and hard to regulate quickly, competitive advantages can persist and entrench, making winner-take-most concentration more likely than AG1 suggests and harming many people and businesses economically.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s complementary jobs and productivity gains prevent economic harm.
objection: The complementary jobs AI creates are often higher-skill and scarcer than the jobs it displaces, so many workers face unemployment, underemployment, or wage pressure rather than broad income protection.

target: AG1’s claim that retraining will let most displaced workers move into complementary roles.
objection: Displaced workers often face major transition frictions—time, cost, credentials, hiring pipelines, and relocation—that prevent smooth reemployment, so AI often causes widespread income loss and job insecurity instead of easy transitions.

target: AG2’s claim that transition frictions make widespread job loss unavoidable.
objection: Higher productivity and lower operating costs can expand production and service scale, increasing demand for labor, and retraining can help many workers move into complementary roles, so widespread job insecurity is not inevitable.

target: AG1’s claim that retraining can generally fill complementary roles.
objection: Complementary jobs often require specialized technical and domain expertise, while retraining pathways are constrained by time, cost, and prerequisites; for many workers, those roles are not realistically reachable through common retraining, so the necessary skills are functionally incompatible with such pathways.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily reduces wages and employment rather than broadening opportunity.
objection: AI can raise productivity, lower costs, expand availability of goods and services, and shift workers into complementary roles, so it can improve real living standards and overall economic well-being instead of causing persistent widespread income loss.

target: AG1’s claim that output expansion will offset lower labor intensity and preserve jobs.
objection: AI can reduce labor-intensity enough that higher output does not translate into proportionally higher labor demand, so employment and income can still fall for many workers even when aggregate consumption rises.

target: AG2’s claim that lower labor-intensity necessarily means lower employment and incomes.
objection: When AI lowers costs and expands market scale enough, total labor demand can rise even if labor per unit falls, and AI also creates complementary work in oversight, integration, maintenance, training, and adaptation, offsetting displacement.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s productivity gains and complementary jobs offset the harms to small firms and workers.
objection: AI development and deployment typically require large-scale data and compute that favor big firms, so competitive advantages concentrate, smaller firms lose opportunities, and aggregate labor-demand gains do not guarantee that the many people and businesses harmed by concentration benefit at all.
